sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Python is a high-level, interpreted language known for its readable syntax. It is widely used in data science and AI.

sections.heading: Variables and Data Types
sections.text: A variable stores a value. Common types are int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, dict and set. Python infers the type from the value.

sections.heading: Control Flow
sections.text: if, elif and else make decisions. for and while loops repeat code.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: for i in range(3): print(i) prints 0, 1 and 2.

sections.heading: Functions
sections.text: def defines a reusable block of code. Use return to send a value back.

sections.heading: Modules
sections.text: import brings in code from other files or libraries, for example import math.

sections.heading: Libraries for AI
sections.text: NumPy handles arrays, pandas handles tables, Matplotlib draws charts and scikit-learn provides machine learning tools.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: def square(x): return x * x. Then square(4) gives 16.

sections.heading: NumPy
sections.text: NumPy provides fast n-dimensional arrays and mathematical functions that work on whole arrays at once.

sections.heading: pandas
sections.text: pandas provides the DataFrame, a table of rows and columns used to load, clean and analyse data.

sections.heading: Common Operations
sections.text: Selecting columns, filtering rows, grouping, handling missing values and merging tables.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: import numpy as np; a = np.array([1, 2, 3]); a * 2 gives [2, 4, 6].

sections.heading: Vectors and Matrices
sections.text: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers. Data sets are often stored as matrices.

sections.heading: Dot Product
sections.text: The dot product of two vectors multiplies matching entries and adds the results. It measures how aligned two vectors are.

sections.heading: Matrix Multiplication
sections.text: An m × n matrix can multiply an n × p matrix to give an m × p matrix. Neural network layers rely on this operation.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: For [1, 2] · [3, 4], the dot product is 1×3 + 2×4 = 11.

sections.heading: Probability
sections.text: Probability measures how likely an event is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

sections.heading: Mean and Variance
sections.text: The mean is the average value. Variance measures how far values spread from the mean. Standard deviation is its square root.

sections.heading: Bayes’ Theorem
sections.text: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). It updates a belief after seeing new evidence.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: The mean of 2, 4 and 6 is (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4.

sections.heading: Derivative
sections.text: A derivative gives the rate of change of a function at a point.

sections.heading: Gradient
sections.text: The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives. It points in the direction of steepest increase.

sections.heading: Gradient Descent
sections.text: Repeatedly update the parameters against the gradient: w = w − η × gradient, where η is the learning rate.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: For f(x) = x², the derivative is 2x, so at x = 3 the slope is 6.

sections.heading: What is Machine Learning?
sections.text: Machine learning lets computers learn patterns from data and use them to make predictions or decisions.

sections.heading: Types of Learning
sections.text: Supervised learning uses labelled data. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards and penalties.

sections.heading: ML Workflow
sections.text: Collect data, clean it, choose features, train a model, evaluate it and then deploy it.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: Predicting house prices from size and location is a supervised regression problem.

sections.heading: Regression and Classification
sections.text: Regression predicts a number. Classification predicts a category.

sections.heading: Common Algorithms
sections.text: Linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, k-nearest neighbours and support vector machines.

sections.heading: Train and Test Split
sections.text: Data is divided so the model is trained on one part and tested on unseen data to check how well it generalises.

sections.heading: Overfitting
sections.text: Overfitting happens when a model memorises the training data and performs poorly on new data. Regularisation and more data help reduce it.

sections.heading: Accuracy
sections.text: Accuracy is the share of predictions that are correct.

sections.heading: Precision and Recall
sections.text: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct. Recall is the share of actual positives that were found.

sections.heading: Cross-Validation
sections.text: The data is split into several folds. The model is trained and tested on different folds to get a more reliable score.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: If 90 of 100 predictions are correct, the accuracy is 90%.

sections.heading: Neuron
sections.text: An artificial neuron takes inputs, multiplies them by weights, adds a bias and passes the result through an activation function.

sections.heading: Layers
sections.text: A network has an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Deep learning uses many hidden layers.

sections.heading: Activation Functions
sections.text: ReLU, sigmoid and tanh add non-linearity so the network can learn complex patterns.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: A neuron with output = ReLU(w·x + b) returns 0 for negative values and the value itself otherwise.

sections.heading: Loss Function
sections.text: The loss measures how far predictions are from the true values, for example mean squared error or cross-entropy.

sections.heading: Backpropagation
sections.text: Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute how the loss changes with each weight.

sections.heading: Optimisers
sections.text: Optimisers such as SGD and Adam update the weights using the gradients.

sections.heading: Epochs and Batches
sections.text: An epoch is one full pass over the training data. A batch is a small group of samples processed together.

sections.heading: Convolutional Neural Networks
sections.text: CNNs use filters that slide over an image to detect edges, shapes and textures. They are widely used for image tasks.

sections.heading: Recurrent Neural Networks
sections.text: RNNs process sequences by passing a hidden state from one step to the next. LSTM and GRU variants handle longer sequences.

sections.heading: Transformers
sections.text: Transformers use attention to relate every word in a sequence to every other word. They power modern language models.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: A CNN can classify a photo as a cat or a dog.

sections.heading: Tokenization
sections.text: Tokenization splits text into smaller units such as words or subwords.

sections.heading: Stop Words
sections.text: Stop words are very common words like the and is. They are often removed because they add little meaning.

sections.heading: Stemming and Lemmatization
sections.text: Stemming chops word endings. Lemmatization reduces a word to its dictionary form, for example running becomes run.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: The sentence Cats are running can be tokenised into Cats, are, running.

sections.heading: Bag of Words
sections.text: Represents a document by counting how often each word appears, ignoring word order.

sections.heading: TF-IDF
sections.text: TF-IDF gives a word a higher score when it is frequent in a document but rare across the whole collection.

sections.heading: Word Embeddings
sections.text: Embeddings such as Word2Vec and GloVe map words to dense vectors where similar words are close together.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: In an embedding space, the vectors for king and queen are close to each other.

sections.heading: Sentiment Analysis
sections.text: Classifies text as positive, negative or neutral.

sections.heading: Named Entity Recognition
sections.text: Finds and labels names of people, places and organisations in text.

sections.heading: Language Models
sections.text: Transformer based models such as BERT and GPT learn language from huge text collections and can be adapted to many tasks.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: A review that says great battery life would be classified as positive.
